Washington, D.C.—Congressman Tom Suozzi (D-NY) today introduced the bipartisan Health Care Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Act with Congresswoman Claudia Tenney (R-NY) to strengthen the federal government’s efforts to combat waste, fraud, and abuse across government healthcare programs. The legislation would increase funding for the Health Care Fraud and Abuse Control Program (HCFAC), a joint agency program involving the Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Office of Inspector General (OIG), Department of Justice, and FBI. HCFAC coordinates federal, state, and local efforts to identify and prosecute health care fraud across programs including Medicare, Medicaid, and other government health care programs.

“Taxpayers bear the cost of every dollar lost to fraud, ultimately making healthcare more expensive. If we want to lower healthcare costs, we need to start by going after waste, fraud, and abuse wherever it’s happening. HCFAC is a tremendously successful program helping us do just that,” said Congressman Suozzi. “Fighting fraud is not a partisan issue; it’s common sense. The Health Care Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Act is about protecting taxpayers, rooting out fraud, and helping keep health care costs down. I’m proud to introduce this important bill to protect taxpayers and the healthcare programs that so many patients depend on.”

“Every dollar stolen through health care fraud is a dollar taken from taxpayers and the patients who depend on these programs,” said Congresswoman Tenney. “Fraudsters are becoming more sophisticated, and the federal government must have the tools and resources to find them, stop them, and hold them accountable. The Health Care Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Act strengthens the investigators and watchdogs on the front lines of this fight and improves oversight across federal health care programs. Protecting Medicare, Medicaid, and other critical programs from fraud will safeguard taxpayer dollars and help ensure these resources are there for the Americans who truly need them.”

Every dollar lost to fraud costs not only the government, but trickles down to consumers through higher premiums and costs on other health care expenses. HCFAC is a highly effective federal program, returning $3 to taxpayers for every dollar spent. By increasing the funding for this successful and worthwhile program, this legislation fights fraud responsibly, by equipping federal agencies with additional resources to prevent fraudulent payments, hold bad actors accountable, lower costs for patients, and recover taxpayer dollars.

Since 2010, the scope of HCFAC’s work has expanded significantly. Medicare and Medicaid spending has far outpaced inflation, enrollment has skyrocketed, and fraudsters have become savvier. The funding for HCFAC has not kept up. As a result, the network of agencies involved have had to police a broader and more complex system without adequate resources. To address this, the Health Care Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Act would rebase HCFAC’s funding, raising it to $490,000,000 for FY2027, $520,000,000 for FY2028, $57,000,000 for FY2029, and ensuring it continues to increase commensurate with inflation in FY2030 and beyond.

###
title: Suozzi Introduces Bipartisan Bill to Crack Down on Health Care Fraud

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Rep. Chu (CA-28), Rep. Sherman (CA-32), Sen. Schiff (D-CA), and Sen. Padilla (D-CA) sent a letter to Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Administrator Cameron Hamilton demanding the agency immediately release outstanding funding for the Disaster Case Management Program (DCMP), which is set to terminate on September 30, 2026.

Nearly twenty months after the devastating Eaton and Palisades Fires, thousands of survivors remain displaced. The DCMP has been a lifeline for many, providing survivors with individualized assistance to navigate FEMA and SBA assistance, insurance claims, temporary housing, and long-term rebuilding plans. The demand for this program remains high: providers report 1,397 open cases and roughly 700 additional survivors on a waitlist, with more than 1,000 active cases involving Eaton Fire survivors alone. DCMP referrals have helped survivors access more than $100 million in direct assistance since January 2025. If the program shuts down, providers estimate 109 case management staff positions will be eliminated.

The looming termination is not due to a lack of approved funding. FEMA has simply failed to release millions of dollars it has already approved for the program. The State of California requested approximately $26 million to operate the program, and FEMA approved roughly $13 million. However, only about $3 million has been paid to date, leaving nearly $10 million in approved funding outstanding. A California Department of Social Services (CDSS) request for approximately $6 million in supplemental funding also remains pending.

"Twenty months after the Eaton Fire devastated our communities, survivors of the 2025 Los Angeles Fires have already waited longer than survivors of any other disaster for long-term federal recovery funding,” said Rep. Chu. Now, FEMA is withholding millions in approved recovery funding, forcing the Disaster Case Management Program to shut down more than a year early while survivors are still waiting for the help they need. Shutting down such a critical lifeline for no reason is indefensible. I'm calling on FEMA to immediately provide the funding necessary to keep these case managers on the job. Eaton Fire survivors and communities across Los Angeles have already lost enough. I will not stop fighting until they have the federal resources they need to rebuild and come home."

“FEMA needs to provide these funds quickly”, said Rep. Sherman. “The Los Angeles wildfires were the costliest in U.S. history, and Congress needs to provide funding for the Disaster Case Management Program (DCMP) so it can accomplish its purpose of providing individualized assistance to fire survivors in accessing federal benefits they qualify for and developing long-term recovery plans.”

The lawmakers are demanding FEMA immediately release the remaining funds under the existing DCMP award and expedite review of CDSS's supplemental funding request.

Read the full letter HERE and below.

--

September 10, 2026

The Honorable Cameron Hamilton

Administrator

Federal Emergency Management Agency

500 C Street SW

Washington, DC 20472

Dear Administrator Hamilton:

We write with urgent concern regarding the impending termination of the Disaster Case Management Program (DCMP) serving survivors of the January 2025 Eaton and Palisades Fires in Los Angeles County. According to the California Department of Social Services (CDSS), the program will be forced to end on September 30, 2026, because the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has not provided sufficient funding to continue operations.

Nearly twenty months after these devastating fires, thousands of survivors remain displaced and continue to face significant barriers to rebuilding their homes and communities. The DCMP provides critical, individualized assistance to survivors navigating the complex recovery process, including accessing FEMA and Small Business Administration assistance, navigating insurance claims, securing temporary housing, identifying rebuilding resources, and developing long-term recovery plans. These services are particularly important for older adults, people with disabilities, individuals with limited English proficiency, and other survivors who may face additional barriers to accessing recovery assistance.

The continued need for these services is clear. DCMP providers report that there are currently 1,397 open cases and approximately 700 additional survivors on a waitlist for case management services. More than 1,000 of the active cases involve Eaton Fire survivors. Since January 2025, providers report that DCMP referrals have helped survivors access more than $100 million in direct assistance. If the program terminates on September 30, providers estimate that approximately 109 DCMP staff positions will be eliminated, disrupting assistance for survivors who are still actively working to recover.

We are particularly concerned by reports regarding the status of federal funding for the program. According to DCMP providers, California initially requested approximately $26 million from FEMA to operate the program. FEMA approved approximately $13 million, but only approximately $3 million has been paid to date, leaving approximately $10 million of the approved award outstanding. We further understand that CDSS has submitted a request for approximately $6 million in supplemental funding to sustain the program through the full period requested by the state.

We therefore urge FEMA to immediately release any remaining funds available under the existing DCMP award and expeditiously review and approve CDSS's pending request for supplemental funding necessary to prevent an interruption in services. FEMA must take all available steps to ensure that survivors do not lose access to their case managers on September 30 simply because federal funding has not been provided in time.

Given the imminent termination of the program, we also request responses to the following questions:

What is preventing FEMA from releasing the remaining funding under the existing DCMP award, and when will those funds be made available to California?

What is the status of CDSS's pending request for approximately $6 million in supplemental funding, and when will FEMA make a determination?

What actions will FEMA take before September 30 to prevent any interruption in case management services for survivors?

The Eaton and Palisades Fires devastated communities across Los Angeles County. With thousands of survivors still displaced and nearly 2,100 households either receiving or waiting for case management assistance, withdrawing this support now would undermine the recovery work that survivors, community organizations, and government agencies have spent nearly twenty months undertaking.

We urge FEMA to act immediately to prevent any interruption in these critical services. Given the September 30 deadline, we request a response to this letter no later than September 18, 2026.
title: Reps. Chu, Sherman, Sens. Schiff, Padilla Demand FEMA Release Withheld Funding for LA Wildfire Case Management Program

Washington, D.C. – Representatives Norma Torres (CA-35) and John Rutherford (FL-05), both members of the House Appropriations Committee that oversees government spending, celebrated the inclusion of a provision in the Fiscal Year 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) Appropriations Report recognizing Blue Envelope Programs as an eligible use of Byrne Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) funding and to highlight these programs nationwide. The report was reported out of the Appropriations Committee last month, and now awaits consideration by the full House.

Blue Envelope programs help improve communication between law enforcement and public safety personnel with individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (I/DD), or others who may face communication challenges.

The report language notes that Blue Envelope Programs are consistent with existing Byrne JAG funding priorities, including law enforcement training and community engagement initiatives. The report also directs the Department of Justice to provide Congress with a report within 180 days on efforts to highlight Blue Envelope Programs to grant recipients.

"This is an important step toward expanding Blue Envelope Programs across the country and ensuring that individuals with autism, developmental disabilities, and communication challenges can have safer and more positive interactions with law enforcement," said Congresswoman Torres. "The inclusion of this language in the House Appropriations report recognizes the value of these programs and encourages awareness and support nationwide. While this progress is worth celebrating, I will continue working with Congressman Rutherford to pass our bipartisan legislation and create a dedicated federal funding stream to help communities establish and expand Blue Envelope Programs."

“As a former sheriff and lifelong law enforcement officer, I know that effective communication is essential to keeping both officers and the people they serve safe,” said Congressman Rutherford. “Recognizing Blue Envelope Programs as an eligible use of Byrne JAG funding is an important step toward helping more law enforcement agencies reduce misunderstandings and improve interactions with individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (I/DD), and others who may face communication challenges. I am proud to work with my colleague Congresswoman Torres to advance this bipartisan effort."

Last December, Congresswoman Torres and Congressman Rutherford introduced the bipartisan Supporting Blue Envelope Programs Act (H.R.6602) to establish a federal grant program that would support the creation, expansion, and implementation of Blue Envelope Programs, which already exist in 29 states, including in California and Florida. Senator Coons (DE) and Schmitt (MO) lead the companion bill in the Senate (S.4089). The bill is supported by numerous law enforcement organizations, stakeholders, and community advocates.

Blue Envelope Programs provide individuals with a clearly identifiable blue envelope that can hold driver's licenses, vehicle registrations, emergency contact information, and other materials that help first responders better understand a person's communication needs during traffic stops and other interactions. Programs may also provide additional tools and training to support effective communication between law enforcement officers and individuals with disabilities.

Background

The FY 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations Report (House Report 119-652) includes language recognizing Blue Envelope Programs as an allowable use of Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funding. The report encourages the Department of Justice to highlight these programs in guidance provided to Byrne JAG grantees and directs the Department to report to Congress within 180 days on its efforts.

In FY 2026, Congresswoman Torres secured $1.031 million in Community Project Funding for the Autism Society Inland Empire, in partnership with the Pomona Police Department, Fontana Police Department, Ontario Police Department, and Chino Police Department, to support specialized law enforcement training for interactions with individuals with ASD, ISD, and other communication challenges.

title: Representatives Torres and Rutherford Secure First Federal Recognition of Blue Envelope Programs in House Appropriations Report

TAMPA, Fla. – U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor (FL-14) today expressed strong opposition to data centers in Hillsborough County in a letter to the Hillsborough County Board of County Commissioners. Castor highlighted the significant strains on pocketbooks and local resources associated with data center development that can drive up electric and water bills for residents, farmers and small businesses.

In Hillsborough County, the average electric utility bill has increased by over 40 percent in the past five years. Castor’s bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act would require data centers to pay the full costs of energy demand and protect ratepayers from data center rate hikes.

Castor concluded, “Data centers cannot come at a cost to neighbors who are already facing high grocery, gas, utility, health care and housing costs. We need to make sure these projects actually bring good-paying jobs to our community and that workers, families, and neighborhoods aren’t forced to pay the burden of rapid technology growth, while out-of-state tech billionaires get richer.”

Read the full letter below:

RE: Opposition to Data Center Development in Hillsborough County

Dear Commissioner[s]:

As the Hillsborough County Board of County Commissioners considers the future of data centers in our community, I would like to relay my strong opposition to the siting of data centers in Hillsborough County. The potential impacts on the cost of living for our residents and on our community’s essential resources are too significant to ignore.

As the Ranking Member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee’s Energy Subcommittee, I have led the national conversation in Congress as we grapple with high energy bills and rising electricity demand from data centers. I’m proud to lead the Ratepayer Protection Act – a bipartisan bill that requires data centers to pay the full costs of their energy demand. Data centers cannot be allowed to pass on their costs to hardworking Florida families and small businesses. The Ratepayer Protection Act would preserve local control over siting and permitting decisions – because these are decisions that should be made by the people and communities where these facilities are being built.

Equally troubling is the immense water usage required for cooling these facilities. In a state where water resources are already under pressure from population growth and climate challenges, diverting millions of gallons for private corporations is neither sustainable nor in the public’s best interest. The county faces moderate to extreme drought conditions, limiting our public water supplies and hurting our farming communities. Hillsborough County and Tampa Bay Water are grappling with huge new water demand requirements and costs. Plant City is already turning to creative water solutions, like reuse for crop freeze protection, and population growth that are threatening local aquifer levels. Community leaders have expressed to me their strong opposition to data centers that could further strain our limited water supplies.

I am also deeply concerned about the new state law permitting nondisclosure agreements for data centers. Secret deals are wrong. This lack of transparency undermines public trust and prevents residents from fully understanding the environmental, economic, and infrastructural impact on their lives. Our community deserves immediate open access to information about developments that could affect our daily lives for decades to come.

Data centers cannot come at a cost to neighbors who are already facing high grocery, gas, utility, health care and housing costs. We need to make sure these projects actually bring good-paying jobs to our community and that workers, families, and neighborhoods aren’t forced to pay the burden of rapid technology growth, while out-of-state tech billionaires get richer.

Please act decisively to protect Hillsborough County’s residents, resources, and long-term sustainability.

I respectfully urge you to prioritize the public interest over private profit.

Thank you for your time, service, and commitment to our community.
title: U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor Opposes Data Centers in Hillsborough County

Minneapolis, MN — Today, Congressman Joaquin Castro (TX-20) released the following statement after visiting Valley View Elementary School in Minneapolis, Minnesota:

“Today I reunited with Liam Conejo Ramos and his father Adrian at his school, Valley View Elementary in Minnesota. The last time I was with them, I was escorting them back home from the Dilley Trailer Prison. Liam's mom was 3 months pregnant at the time. Today, I met Liam's new brother.

“Liam, the boy with the bunny hat and spiderman backpack, was one of many children who were taken during Operation Metro Surge. Today, I met with one such student and her family. She and her mom spent over 50 days at Dilley. She dreams of becoming a doctor. Both families shared their stories with me. They didn’t receive a proper meal when they arrived. They had nothing with them—no comforts from home. They had done nothing wrong and didn’t know why they were taken and locked away.

“The suffering does not end when children leave Dilley. It inflicts lasting trauma.

“Thank you to Antonio Tijerino of the Hispanic Heritage Foundation for joining me and to everyone at Liam's school. I am deeply grateful to the teachers and staff at Valley View Elementary School and the administrators at Columbia Heights Public Schools. You are doing an extraordinary job making school a place for learning, not fear.

“Kids deserve to be kids. We need to shut down Dilley and end child detention in America.”
title: Congressman Castro Reunites with Liam Conejo Ramos, Tours Minneapolis Elementary School

NORTH JERSEY — Today, September 10, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) announced $1.7 million clawed-back for eight nonprofit organizations across North Jersey for Fiscal Year 2025 Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP) funding, delivering critical resources to help churches, synagogues, temples, and faith-based schools in the Fifth District protect their communities from the growing threat of hate and violence. Gottheimer also announced the funding at Bris Avrohom of Fair Lawn and visited Rabbi Mendel Zaltzman and Rabbi Mordechai Kanelsky ahead of the High Holidays.

See video of Gottheimer’s visit here.

Gottheimer also hosted a briefing with the New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness (NJOHSP) and Jewish faith leaders from across North Jersey to address the security threats facing the Jewish community as they prepare for the High Holidays. The meeting brought together NJOHSP Director Hauck, state leadership, and Jewish faith leaders to discuss the current threat landscape, coordination between law enforcement and religious institutions, and the urgent need to deliver federal security resources to houses of worship — the very resources this NSGP funding provides.

Gottheimer has been pushing for the long-delayed resources, passed in 2024, to be distributed after clawing it back for the district. The Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP), administered by the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), provides funding to nonprofits at high risk of terrorist attacks or hate-related incidents, with a particular focus on houses of worship and other faith-based institutions like schools and community centers. The funding allows organizations to invest in physical security upgrades like cameras, gates, bollards, and blast-resistant film, and to provide training that helps staff and congregants recognize and respond to threats.

Anti-Jewish hate crimes account for nearly two-thirds of all religion-based hate crimes reported to the FBI nationwide. Antisemitic incidents in the United States have increased by 68% since 2022, before October 7. In 2025, ADL recorded 6,274 antisemitic incidents across the United States. That means Jewish Americans were targeted an average of 17 times per day. New Jersey recorded the third-highest total of antisemitic incidents across the nation in 2025, with Bergen County ranking first in highest rates of antisemitic incidents in New Jersey.

Gottheimer has been a vocal advocate for this vital funding to be distributed. Last year, Gottheimer led a bipartisan group of 78 colleagues in urging the Administration to reverse its decision to pause the drawdown of federal grant funding at FEMA, which includes the Nonprofit Security Grant Program.

“No one should ever have to worry about their safety while praying, learning, or gathering with their community,” said Congressman Gottheimer (NJ-5). “With hate crimes and antisemitic incidents spiking at historical levels, this funding is crucial. It gives our religious communities the resources they need to strengthen their security and protect the people who walk through their doors every day. I’ll keep fighting in Washington to make sure North Jersey’s nonprofits and religious institutions get every dollar they need to stay safe.”

The following North Jersey organizations were awarded funding:

Bris Avrohom of Fair Lawn (Fair Lawn) — $380,000

Young Israel of Fort Lee (Fort Lee) — $190,000

Grace Redeemer Church (Glen Rock) — $190,000

Hindu Samaj Temple of Mahwah (Mahwah) — $175,750

The Frisch School (Paramus) — $380,000

The Church Gathered and Scattered (Teaneck) — $95,000

The Young Israel of Teaneck (Teaneck) — $190,000

Temple Emanuel of the Pascack Valley (Woodcliff Lake) — $190,000

Gottheimer will continue working in Congress to protect and expand funding for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program and push FEMA for faster turnaround and greater transparency so that at-risk organizations can plan and receive their security investments with confidence.

Washington, D.C. – Today, Representatives Mark DeSaulnier (CA-10) and Jimmy Patronis (FL-01) introduced the Sunset Section 230 Act, which would repeal Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996, making it possible for Americans to bring legal action against big tech companies responsible for online harm.

“With one in five American teenagers reporting harm to their mental health from social media sites, it is critical and urgent that we take action to rein in the big tech companies that are allowing the dissemination of harmful material on their platforms. These companies have been profiting at the expense of young people, who have been harassed and subjected to harmful content,” said Congressman DeSaulnier. “This legislation combined with the recent legal action against companies like Meta should send a loud message: Big Tech’s days of acting with impunity, wreaking havoc, and then asking for forgiveness once the damage has been done are over.”

“Big Tech has become a crooked dealer, pushing digital fentanyl to our kids while profiting from their addiction. Enough is enough. I’m proud to partner with Congressman DeSaulnier to co-lead the Sunset Section 230 Act and fight to repeal Section 230 once and for all. It’s time to hold Big Tech accountable and put our kids’ safety ahead of Big Tech’s profits,” said Congressman Patronis.

Section 230 was created in 1996 as part of the Communications Decency Act to help encourage innovation and growth among new social media companies, but 30 years later as these companies have become inordinately powerful, Section 230 has become obsolete and dangerous. By sunsetting Section 230 after two years, this bill would provide much needed reform to our tech policy that would protect all users of social media, particularly children, from harmful content and hold companies responsible for demonstrated injury to users of their platforms.

Introduction of this legislation comes as Meta agreed this summer to pay up to $18 billion to settle claims brought by 29 U.S. states that the company had contributed to the national youth mental health crisis. The deal also mandates that Meta introduce new guardrails for young users of its platforms, including default daily time limits and nighttime blocks that can only be lifted by a parent, an enhanced mechanism for teens to report potentially harmful content and a requirement that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours, and bans on features such as cosmetic procedure image filters and the display of the numbers of likes on posts. Earlier this year, Meta suffered additional losses in court over claims it created addictive products that harmed young Americans.

Full text of the bill can be found here.

Congressman DeSaulnier is a senior member of the House Committee on Education & Workforce and a longtime advocate for consumer safety and the health and wellbeing of young people, having sponsored legislation to hold e-cigarette companies accountable for their role in the youth vaping crisis and to increase access to supports, services, and resources for children, students, workers, and families by strengthening school-based behavioral health care, bolstering mental health parity protections, and ensuring access to mental health and substance use disorder benefits for workers and families.
title: Representatives DeSaulnier and Patronis Introduce Legislation to Hold Tech Companies Accountable and Protect Young Americans

In response to President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14399 seeking to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01), co-chair of the Congressional Postal Caucus, led 99 members in calling on the Postmaster General to revoke a Postal Service rule codifying the order. In addition to that, Pappas joined a bipartisan coalition in filing an amicus brief to the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al., a lawsuit brought by a coalition of State Attorneys General against the U.S. Postal Service.

One-third of Americans are expected to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections—a voting practice Donald Trump himself used as recently as August 2026, when the president voted in Florida’s Republican primary. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found an average of just four cases of voter fraud for every 10 million mail-in ballots cast — and that states using universal mail-in voting have among the lowest fraud rates in the country.

Letter to Postmaster General David P. Steiner:

Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01), Congresswoman Nikki Budzinski (IL-13), and Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08) led 97 colleagues in calling on Postmaster General David P. Steiner to revoke a Postal Service rule that codifies President Trump's Executive Order targeting vote-by-mail.

“The evidence is clear: voting by mail is safe, effective, and helps to ensure everyone is able to execute their constitutional right to vote. USPS has played an essential role in elections for generations – and it is our fear that this final rule risks harming the democratic process and severely damaging USPS’s relationship with the millions of Americans who rely on USPS to deliver ballots every election cycle,” the members wrote.

The lawmakers warn that if the rule survives legal challenge, it would carry real consequences: disrupting operations for tens of thousands of USPS employees, creating new obstacles for tens of millions of voters who rely on mail-in ballots, and further eroding public trust in the electoral process.

Amicus brief to the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al.:

Congressman Pappas joined a court filing challenging the legality of President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14399. The court case challenges a Final Rule issued by the USPS pursuant to Trump’s directive that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

In the court filing, the amici curiae argue that the order violates the separation of powers and usurps congressional authorities outlined in Article I of the U.S. Constitution, which gives the states and Congress exclusive authority over election administration.

“As current and former legislators, amici took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States—including its guarantee of the separation of powers. Amici have a particular interest in defending the institutional role of the Legislative Branch under Article I of the Constitution and in vindicating the long-settled principle that the Constitution commits ultimate regulatory authority over federal elections to Congress. The Constitution does not contemplate the Executive Branch acting unilaterally to assert power over federal elections. Yet that is what the Order and Final Rule do,” wrote the lawmakers.
title: Pappas Fights Back on Trump’s Executive Order Limiting Mail-In Voting

WASHINGTON — On Wednesday, Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) demanded that the Department of Transportation and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration take immediate action to address the misuse of Tesla’s Autopilot and Full Self-Driving systems after an NBC News investigation identified dozens of videos appearing to show Tesla driver asleep or otherwise disengaged behind the wheel while their vehicles were moving.

In a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Krishnamoorthi cited an NBC News investigation that identified 43 videos appearing to show individuals asleep in the driver’s seat of moving Teslas, including 17 posted this year alone. Tesla’s own documentation states that Autopilot and Full Self-Driving require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems.

In the letter, Krishnamoorthi writes:

“A recent NBC News investigation identified 43 videos that appear to show individuals asleep in the driver’s seat of moving Teslas, including 17 posted this year alone. These incidents are particularly alarming because Autopilot and FSD require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems. As these technologies become increasingly prevalent on American roads, DOT and NHTSA must ensure that manufacturers have adequate safeguards to prevent foreseeable misuse and that drivers are not encouraged to place dangerous levels of reliance on systems that still require their full attention.”

Krishnamoorthi noted that NHTSA has previously identified shortcomings in Tesla’s driver-engagement safeguards. In an earlier engineering analysis of Autopilot, the agency concluded that Tesla’s system did not sufficiently ensure that drivers remained attentive and used the technology appropriately, identifying a mismatch between Autopilot’s substantial control over the vehicle and its safeguards for keeping drivers engaged.

NBC News also reported on videos appearing to show Tesla drivers sleeping at highway speeds, using laptops, watching videos, and otherwise disengaging while FSD was operating. NBC News also reported that some drivers said they had been able to evade the cabin-camera monitoring system, including by wearing sunglasses or obstructing the camera.

Krishnamoorthi also raised concerns about messages Tesla reportedly began displaying to drivers with software update 2025.32.3. WIRED reported that those messages included “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD” and “Lane drift detected. Let FSD assist so you can stay focused.” Because FSD requires continuous human supervision, Krishnamoorthi questioned whether encouraging a driver whom the vehicle has already detected as drowsy to use the system creates an additional safety risk.

In the letter, Krishnamoorthi writes:

“Advising an alert driver who experiences a momentary lane drift to use a driver-assistance feature is one thing. Encouraging a driver whom the vehicle has detected as drowsy to ‘stay focused with FSD’ presents a fundamentally different safety question. FSD requires continuous human supervision, yet the message appears to encourage use of the system precisely when the vehicle has detected that the driver may be less capable of providing that supervision.”

The concerns come as NHTSA conducts an ongoing engineering analysis involving approximately 3.2 million Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD. The agency is examining whether FSD’s degradation-detection system can identify reduced roadway visibility and provide drivers with an adequate warning and sufficient time to respond. The investigation identifies nine incidents, including one fatality and one injury.

Krishnamoorthi is demanding answers to the following questions:

Is NHTSA aware of the growing body of publicly available videos showing Tesla drivers apparently asleep or otherwise disengaged from the driving task while Autopilot or FSD is operating? Has the agency assessed whether these incidents indicate a systemic problem with Tesla’s driver-monitoring or driver-engagement systems?

Has NHTSA communicated with Tesla regarding videos depicting drivers sleeping, using laptops, watching video, gaming, or otherwise disengaging from the driving task while FSD is operating? If so, what information has Tesla provided regarding the frequency of such behavior and the effectiveness of its safeguards?

What data has NHTSA collected or requested from Tesla—through the Standing General Order or other authorities—concerning driver inattention, drowsiness, or apparent driver disengagement in crashes involving Autopilot or FSD? How many such incidents has the agency identified since January 1, 2024?

What is NHTSA’s current assessment of the effectiveness of Tesla’s cabin-camera-based driver-monitoring system? Specifically, has the agency evaluated its performance when the cabin camera is obstructed, visibility is impaired, or drivers use sunglasses, hats, or other means that may interfere with detection?

What findings would lead NHTSA to conclude that Tesla’s driver-monitoring or driver-engagement systems constitute a safety defect requiring corrective action, including a safety recall?

Krishnamoorthi requested a written response by September 30, 2026.
title: Krishnamoorthi Demands NHTSA Action After Tesla Drivers Caught Sleeping Behind the Wheel With Driver-Assistance System Engaged System Engaged

NEWS: Government Watchdog Finds Defense Department is Robbing Workers of Fair Wages and Benefits
WASHINGTON – Today, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a new report on the Department of Defense’s (DOD) use of Intergovernmental Support Agreements (IGSAs) to obtain services from state and local governments and the impact on the workers employed under these contracts.
Requested by House Committee on Education and Workforce Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03) and Rep. Lucy McBath (GA-06), the report revealed that the intergovernmental support agreements adopted by DOD are undermining worker protections under the McNamara-O’Hara Service Contract Act and robbing contract workers of fair wages and benefits.
The McNamara-O’Hara Service Contract Act (SCA) has long provided protections to ensure that unionized firms are not disadvantaged in competition for federal contracts and that these contracts provide wages consistent with prevailing local standards. GAO found that the military services’ use of IGSAs has increased dramatically in recent years. In 2018, GAO reported that 45 IGSAs had been approved across all DOD installations. That number increased to 316 in 2025.
The report examined at the minimum hourly wages for five positions and found that the minimum wages for three of the five positions under IGSAs were lower than the minimum hourly wage required under SCA, raising concerns that IGSAs are being used simply as a loophole to avoid complying with federal law. The report also found that DOD does not always conduct required cost-benefit analyses for prospective IGSAs.
“The McNamara-O’Hara Service Contract Act (SCA) was adopted by Congress to prevent the exploitation of workers by employers looking to win federal contracts by simply offering the lowest bids. Today’s GAO report shows that not only is the Department of Defense using intergovernmental support agreements (IGSAs) to bypass the law, but it is also relying on them,” said Ranking Member Scott. “While the DOD may argue that IGSAs save the government money, it comes at the cost of shortchanging workers of fair wages and decent benefits.”
"After hearing from workers in Georgia, I partnered with Ranking Member Scott to examine the increasing number of Intergovernmental Support Agreements on military bases across the country. 3 out of the 5 of the jobs examined in the report paid workers less than they would have under the Service Contract Act. The Government Accountability Office also found that there was no way to verify the accuracy of cost savings reported by these agreements,” said Rep. McBath. "Working people deserve to be paid what they are owed. The Department of Defense should not exploit legal loopholes to pay workers less. I look forward to doing more with my colleagues in Congress to raise wages for American families."
To read the full report, entitled, “DOD Installation Services: Action Needed to Improve Oversight of Intergovernmental Support Agreements,” click here.

Toledo, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, announced that three Northwest Ohio organizations will receive awards totaling $3.75 Million through the US Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Family Assistance, through its Responsible Fatherhood Program. They teachparenting classes through the Nurturing Fathers program, and they provide extensive economic and vocational support to fathers. The Ridge Project serves families navigating the justice system, whether a member of the family is incarcerated or on probation. Their award will support its TYRO Fathers program, which equips fathers with life, job, and parenting skills for becoming strongly involved in their families’ lives. Serving the Toledo-area community, Pathway provides numerous services to reduce poverty. They serve families, seniors, and individuals with disabilities, and their award will be used to support their Brothers United program.

These new Federal investments build on similar previous awards to communities across our Northwest Ohio region. Just last year, Congresswoman Kaptur secured a combined total of more than $3.7 Million for three responsible fatherhood programs through the US Department of Health and Human Services.

Above: Gottheimer unveils 9/11 legislation package.

NEW MILFORD, NJ — Today, Wednesday, September 9, 2026, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) announced several concrete actions including more than $5 million clawed back from Washington to Jersey for local law enforcement in North Jersey to combat terrorism.

Watch Gottheimer’s remarks here.

The new funding will go toward expanding and modernizing intelligence and coordination, officer training, and additional resources to protect Jersey families.

The resources include:

More than $5 million in counterterrorism funding clawed back for local law enforcement across Bergen, Sussex, and Passaic Counties.

Every single town — all 65 in the Fifth Congressional District — in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties — will receive $50,000 to be utilized for counter-terrorism training.

$1.5 million dollars for Bergen County to expand and modernize the Bergen County Real-Time Intelligence Center.

Newton in Sussex County will receive $200,000 in funding to be able to purchase a real-time intelligence platform to enhance its capabilities.

Bloomingdale will receive $100,000 to purchase a response drone and active-threat gear — ballistic shields, armor, breaching kits.

Vernon will receive $30,000 in funding for a thermal search-and-overwatch drone for fast response at any time of day or conditions.

Highlighted the bipartisan 9/11 Review Task Force Report that lays out twenty bipartisan recommendations for the Intelligence Community to protect against the new and emerging threats — including faster information sharing between agencies, adopting AI to stay ahead of our enemies, and deeper partnerships with our state, local, and private-sector partners to fight terror.

Sent a letter pressing the FAA and Secretary Duffy to fully implement secondary flight deck barriers on all commercial aircraft — the only 9/11 Commission recommendation still not fully implemented 25 years later — to require the barriers on every plane, including older aircraft already flying. In 2018, I wrote the bipartisan Saracini Aviation Safety Act, requiring these barriers on all new aircraft and it was signed into law in 2018. Years later, the FAA still hasn’t finalized the rule to retrofit the existing fleet.

Introduced a 9/11 education bill with Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY-21) to ensure that 9/11 is taught in every school across America. Only 15 states require 9/11 education.

Introduced a resolution, cosponsored by every member of the New Jersey House congressional delegation, formally recognizing the state’s law enforcement officers, firefighters, and emergency medical personnel who responded to the World Trade Center attacks and carried out the rescue, recovery, and relief efforts in the days and months that followed. The resolution honors their service and sacrifice, remembers those who have since died — including from 9/11-related illnesses — and reaffirms the federal commitment to the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund.

“We all have a responsibility, in honor of those who gave their lives, and for the sake of our democracy, to teach our children, our students, and our future leaders the history of our homeland,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “Today, I unveiled a package of federal action that lays out a series of steps we must take to not only honor those who perished on 9/11 and in its aftermath, but to be prepared to stop any future attacks. With today’s actions, we will keep fighting to protect our state, our homeland, and ensure that a tragic day like that one in September of 2001 never happens again.”

Gottheimer was joined by Bergen County Prosecutor Mark Musella, Sussex County Prosecutor Dan Perez, New Milford Mayor Michael Putrino, New Milford Councilwoman Lisa Sandhusen, New Milford Councilwoman Randi Duffie, New Milford Councilman Matt Seymour, Bloomingdale Councilman David Bronkhurst, Newton Police Chief Dan Finkle, Vernon Mayor Anthony Rossi, Vernon Police Chief Daniel Young, Sussex County Chief of Detectives Nicholas T. Elmo, Sussex County Lieutenant Kyle Phlegar, Sussex County Detective Andrew Moore, Bergen County Executive Jim Tedesco, Bergen County Commissioner Germaine Ortiz.

Below: Gottheimer unveils 9/11 legislation package.

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery:

Good morning, everyone.

Twenty-five years ago, this week, New Milford lost one of its own.

Stephen Dorf (DOOR-F) was 39 years old. He worked as a communications technician for Euro Brokers, on the 84th floor of the South Tower.

Stephen was one of six kids in a close-knit family from Brooklyn, and by every account I’ve read, he was exactly the kind of guy you’d want as a neighbor and friend. He was the neighbor grilling in the backyard, the guy who’d give you the shirt off his back if you needed it. That’s who New Milford and Jersey lost on September 11, 2001. Not a statistic. Not a name on a wall. A friend from this remarkable community and our great state.

The steel beam behind us from the towers, the plaque, this plot of land — they mean something. Because behind them is a piece of New Milford’s story that this town will never be torn down.

Because of 9/11, and the havoc monsters wreaked that day, we have memorials like this one across our state and country. I’ve prayed at beautiful memorials like this one more times than I can count over the years. They are both powerful remembrances of our loved ones, a reminder of the strength of our democracy and the flag we pledge to, the indefatigable will of our people, and, in our hours of need, our ability to come together as a nation.

Last week, I was at memorials at the Pentagon, in Lower Manhattan, in Shanksville — and every time, I think about the same thing: the people we lost and their families.

The nearly 3,000 souls that day, and the 750 who called New Jersey home. One hundred and forty-seven from Bergen County alone.

I think about the passengers on Flight 93, who fought back over a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, so that plane never reached its target — the United States Capitol. They literally came together and voted, on the spot, to swap their lives for the terrorists — to protect us.

I think about the more than 400 first responders who ran into those towers instead of running away — because that’s what they do, and that’s what they still do, every day, right here in New Milford.

And I think about something that doesn’t get said enough: more than 9,000 first responders and survivors have died from illnesses tied to what they breathed in at Ground Zero. That is three times the number of people who died on the day of the attack itself. I think about the 60,000 servicemen and women who gave their lives in or were injured in the War on Terror in Iraq and Afghanistan.

For those of us who lived through this tragedy, where we were and how we learned about the attacks is seared in our memory. But, twenty-five years is a long time.

It’s long enough that we have college students graduating this spring who weren’t alive for 9/11. We have educators in our classrooms who weren’t alive. 100 million Americans have been born since that tragic morning — nearly a third of our country. Their only connection to that day is a memorial like this one, a story from their parents, a paragraph in a textbook, if they’re lucky enough to get a paragraph at all.

So, when we say never forget, we all have a responsibility, in honor of those who gave their lives, and for the sake of our democracy, to teach our children, our students, our future leaders the history of our homeland. Otherwise, TikTok will do it — and they may say what the most despicable people are posting and what some of our enemies are spreading — that 9/11 was our fault. I will do everything in my power, and I know you will, too, to ensure that our children learn the truth, honor the fallen, and protect the greatest country the world has ever known.

But that takes work. In 2004, the 9/11 Commission published a report with clear steps to help prevent another terror attack on our soil. As a result, Congress established the National Counterterrorism Center. We created the Director of National Intelligence. We built a system where our intelligence agencies can escape their silos and share information – it was one of the great weaknesses that contributed to the attack that day.

Twenty years later, there is still one 9/11 Commission recommendation — just one — that has never been fully carried out: secondary barriers, to keep terrorists out of the cockpit on every commercial flight in America. Many of us have been working on that for years – but we’re still not there, and there’s no excuse for the airlines’ failure to fully meet that demand. And, there is still work to be done to make sure threats are better shared between our intelligence agencies, especially as they develop faster and grow more sophisticated

As we’ve said, twenty-five years is a long time. America is facing new threats that didn’t exist in 2001, like Artificial Intelligence and the government of China.

For the past year, I served as Co-Chair of the House Intelligence Committee’s bipartisan 9/11 Review Task Force, with Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, Chairman Rick Crawford, and Ranking Member Jim Himes. We spent a year in hearings and briefings, grading our own government’s homework: how well did we actually carry out the original 9/11 Commission’s recommendations, what worked and what didn’t — and how do we prepare for the next generation of threats.

Our report [hold up a copy] lays out twenty bipartisan recommendations to close the gaps for the next 25 years. Things like faster information sharing between agencies, adopting AI to stay ahead of our enemies, and deeper partnerships with our state, local, and private-sector partners to fight terror.

Today, I want to lay out a series of steps we must take to not only honor those who perished on 9/11 and its aftermath, but to be prepared to stop any future attacks.

The first step starts here, in our communities, and it’s about ensuring that our towns and first responders have the resources they need to protect our families here in Bergen, Sussex, and Passaic Counties. This morning, I’m announcing $5 million in new federal counter-terrorism resources that I secured for every community in the Fifth District.

Every single town — all 65 in the Fifth Congressional District — in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties — will receive $50,000 to be utilized for counter-terrorism training — to be prepared for any threats, especially the new ones. That’s $3.25 million in new training dollars.

That funding will allow our towns to receive advanced tactical training for responding to active shooters and violent threats. New specialized training will help identify and mitigate threats to our schools and houses of worship, and it will ensure the maximum number of officers can receive this crucial training without impacting day-to-day operations.

What worked twenty-five years ago doesn’t work today. We must invest in our first responders so they can protect themselves and our families.

In addition, to ensure we are prepared and coordinating, we are investing more than 1.5 million dollars here in Bergen County to expand and modernize the Bergen County Real-Time Intelligence Center. That’s the hub that connects more than 70 law enforcement, fire, and EMS agencies countywide — to better integrate and coordinate emergency response across the county.

The Intelligence Center ensures that agencies don’t miss a beat when a thief flees from one town to the next, and all hands will be on deck for major events at MetLife Stadium.

As part of the federal dollars I secured, Newton in Sussex County will be able to purchase a real-time intelligence platform and help existing systems that aren’t connected. Vernon will receive funding for a thermal search-and-overwatch drone for fast response at any time of day or conditions. And Bloomingdale will receive dollars to purchase a response drone and active-threat gear — ballistic shields, armor, breaching kits. Those are major tools — major federal investments — in the hands of the men and women who are the first on the scene when we need them most – to handle any major threat thrown at them, including terror.

My hope is that all of our communities and agencies will be able to work hand-in-hand, locally, seamlessly, across the state, and with federal partners. That is so critical and one of our biggest lessons from the original 9/11 report and our review.

Second, I’m sending an urgent letter to the FAA and Secretary of Transportation Duffy to finally finish the job on secondary cockpit barriers. Years ago, I wrote the bipartisan Saracini Aviation Safety Act, requiring these barriers on all new aircraft. It was signed into law in 2018.

I then helped pass legislation to require the barriers on every plane — including older aircraft already flying. Yet, years later, the FAA still hasn’t finalized the rule to retrofit the existing fleet. When it finally happens, it will take years to implement. We need the FAA to implement a final rule and get every plane in our skies equipped with a secondary cockpit barrier.

It makes no sense for flight attendants to drag a drink cart into the aisle when the pilot needs to leave the cockpit to use the restroom.

We know that won’t work if a terrorist wants it — studies show that they will literally push over the cart.

Third, I’m leading a resolution this week with the entire New Jersey Congressional House delegation formally honoring New Jersey’s 9/11 first responders. The cops, the firefighters, the EMTs who ran toward the towers, who searched the rubble for months afterward, drawn from all twenty-one of our counties. The ones who helped run the largest waterborne evacuation in American history, carrying an estimated half a million people to safety across the Hudson.

This resolution remembers them, and it reaffirms our commitment to funding the World Trade Center Health Program and the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for as long as they’re needed.

Finally, this step addresses what I discussed at the beginning of my remarks. With my colleague Congresswoman Elise Stefanik of New York, I just introduced a bipartisan bill to ensure that 9/11 is taught in every classroom in America. Not on TikTok, but in our textbooks.

Why? Because if a generation of kids grows up not understanding what happened that day, and why, we haven’t just failed the memory of those lost. We’ve failed the future, we’ve our democracy, and our ability to protect our country. I will not let that happen. Only fifteen states have a requirement to teach about 9/11 – and, believe it or not, New Jersey isn’t one of them. We should change that today, and, in the meantime, I will fill that gap with bipartisan federal legislation.

Twenty-five years ago, I remember, like a lot of you probably do, watching President Bush stand on a pile of smoking rubble at Ground Zero, grab a bullhorn, and shout back to rescue workers who couldn’t hear him: “I can hear you. The rest of the world hears you.” Out of the worst morning in this country’s history, that’s what America decided to be — loud, united, and unafraid.

That’s the New Jersey I know. That’s the New Milford I know. A place where our memory and our pride outlast fear. A place where a guy named Stephen Dorf, who just wanted to go to work and come home to his family, will never, ever be forgotten.

With today’s actions — with real funding, a real report, and real legislation — with the best first responders in the country, the best service men and women, and intelligence officers in the world, we will keep fighting to protect our state, our homeland, and ensure that a tragic day like that one in September of 2001 never happens again.

Because in the greatest country in the world, I know that if we work together, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you. God bless you, God bless our first responders, and God bless the United States of America.
title: RELEASE: Ahead of the 25th Anniversary of 9/11, Gottheimer Announces More Than $5 Million in Federal Funds to Combat Terrorism

Washington, D.C. – United States Representative Jimmy Panetta (CA-19) and more than 250 current and former Members of Congress, Democrats and Republicans, filed an amicus brief challenging the President’s Executive Order seeking to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

The group, made up of a bipartisan, bicameral coalition of 261 lawmakers, filed an amicus brief with the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al., a lawsuit brought by a coalition of state attorneys general against the U.S. Postal Service (USPS). The court case challenges a Final Rule issued by the USPS pursuant to the President’s directive that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

One-third of Americans are expected to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections, a voting practice the President himself used as recently as August 2026, when he voted in Florida’s Republican primary.

In the court filing, the amici curiae argue that the President’s Executive Order 14399, “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” violates the separation of powers and usurps congressional authorities outlined in Article I of the U.S. Constitution, which gives the states and Congress exclusive authority over election administration.

“As current and former legislators, amici took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States—including its guarantee of the separation of powers. Amici have a particular interest in defending the institutional role of the Legislative Branch under Article I of the Constitution and in vindicating the long-settled principle that the Constitution commits ultimate regulatory authority over federal elections to Congress. The Constitution does not contemplate the Executive Branch acting unilaterally to assert power over federal elections. Yet that is what the Order and Final Rule do,” wrote the lawmakers.

The amici also point to a recent federal court ruling blocking the USPS from implementing its newly finalized mail ballot rule for the midterm elections, saying the agency lacked the authority to implement the rule and that its actions are “substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law.”

“The district court correctly concluded that Appellees are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims that USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule, that the Final Rule unconstitutionally imposes mail-ballot requirements on the States, and that the Final Rule unconstitutionally bars non-compliant State and local election officials from using the USPS to mail ballots at all,” continued the lawmakers.

The group concluded by asserting states’ power to administer elections and Congress’s power to make or alter rules regulating elections, which the Supreme Court itself has described as an “override” authority.

“The integrity of our constitutional system depends on each branch keeping to its assigned role. The Framers set up a two-part system that gave the States default authority to regulate federal elections subject to Congress’s authority to override the States. The Framers did not provide the President with any authority to interfere in that system, nor has Congress imbued the Executive Branch with any such authority by statute,” concluded the lawmakers.

The effort was led by House Administration Ranking Member Joe Morelle (NY-25); Assistant House Minority Leader Joe Neguse (CO-02), who leads the House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force; and Task Force Co-Chairs House Oversight Ranking Member Robert Garcia (CA-42) and House Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (MD-08). In the Senate, the brief was championed by Rules Committee Ranking Member Alex Padilla (D-CA); Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY); Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-IL); and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gary Peters (D-MI).

The full brief is available here.

###
title: Rep. Panetta Part of Major Bipartisan Effort to Urge Supreme Court to Block Executive Order Limiting Mail Voting

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Last week, U.S. Representatives Deborah Ross (NC-02) and Ami Bera, M.D. (CA-06) introduced the SERVICE for America Act, which creates a pathway to lawful permanent residency for Dreamers and Documented Dreamers who work in public service.

For many Dreamers and Documented Dreamers, the United States is the only home they have ever known. They went to school here, built careers here, and contribute to our communities, but despite putting down roots, they continue to face uncertainty about whether they will be able to remain in the country they call home.

The SERVICE for America Act would give eligible Dreamers and Documented Dreamers who work in public service a pathway to lawful permanent residency. Qualifying public service includes careers in healthcare, education, public safety, military service, social work, early childhood education, government, and nonprofits. It would also expand opportunities for eligible young immigrants to serve through AmeriCorps.

“Those who dedicate themselves to serving our communities and the country they call home deserve the opportunity to build their futures here,” said Representative Ross. “Our country needs more social workers, teachers, servicemembers, and caretakers. Dreamers and Documented Dreamers are stepping up to fill these roles. It’s past time to fix our broken immigration system and give these young people a pathway to lawful permanent residency. I’m proud to introduce legislation to ensure Dreamers and Documented Dreamers can remain in this country and continue using their talents to make our communities stronger.”

“Dreamers and Documented Dreamers are already giving back to our country as teachers, healthcare workers, servicemembers, and public servants,” said Representative Bera. “They are stepping up, serving their communities, and doing their part to make our country stronger. The SERVICE for America Act creates an earned pathway to permanent residency and gives these young people the certainty and peace of mind they deserve as they continue to build their futures in America.”

“We appreciate the introduction of the Service for America Act, which will allow many long term immigrants who grew up here and are fully contributing to our country, to receive a sense of permanency. Many children of long term visa holders who grew up here lawfully, but age out of their pending green card applications due to backlogs, would be afforded a pathway to stay and contribute in the only country they’ve called home,” said Dip Patel, Founder of Improve The Dream.

The full text of the SERVICE for America Act can be found HERE.

title: Reps. Ross, Bera Introduce the SERVICE for America Act to Provide Pathway to Permanent Residency for Dreamers + Documented Dreamers in Public Service

JERSEY CITY, NJ – Congressional Hispanic Caucus ("CHC") Vice Chair of Policy Rob Menendez (NJ-08), CHC Chair Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), and U.S. Representative Analilia Mejia (NJ-11) today conducted an oversight visit at Delaney Hall, operated by GEO Group, following repeated complaints regarding conditions inside the detention facility, including reports of spoiled food, inadequate or non-functioning air conditioning, and grave concerns about access to timely and appropriate medical care.

Following the visit, the members issued the following joint statement:

“ICE and GEO Group have a responsibility to the people they are holding in federal custody. What we heard and observed today makes clear that those held in Delaney Hall continue to be dangerously neglected.

We met with individuals who detailed medical care being delayed or denied when people are sick or in pain, spoiled and unsafe food being served, and inadequate air conditioning leaving people to endure dangerous conditions. This is a federally funded failure of care and oversight.

We will continue to demand clear answers about what is happening inside this facility, including the deaths of individuals held at Delaney, what DHS is doing to address these conditions, and why people in federal custody have been forced to endure them in the first place.”

The members will continue to review information gathered during today’s visit and pursue additional oversight as warranted, including seeking answers from federal officials and facility operators regarding the conditions reported at Delaney Hall.
title: Menendez, Espaillat, and Mejia Conduct Oversight Visit at Delaney Hall Following Reports of Negligent Conditions

CAGUAS, Puerto Rico - El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández envió una carta a la Oficina para el Desarrollo Socioeconómico y Comunitario de Puerto Rico (ODSEC) sobre posibles retrasos en el desembolso y la administración de fondos federales del programa Community Services Block Grant (CSBG), un programa federal que financia organizaciones comunitarias que ayudan a familias de bajos ingresos a conseguir empleo, estudiar y estabilizar su vivienda, entre otras medidas de bienestar social.

ODSEC es la agencia principal responsable de administrar y distribuir más de $29 millones en fondos federales del programa CSBG en Puerto Rico. Durante el año fiscal federal 2023, el programa CSBG brindó servicios a 24,786 personas de bajos ingresos en Puerto Rico, pertenecientes a 17,162 familias. Los servicios financiados produjeron más de 2,300 resultados relacionados con empleo, más de 2,000 resultados educativos y más de 800 resultados vinculados con ingresos, activos y bienestar financiero.

El Comisionado Residente reveló que documentos revisados por su oficina indican que al menos una de las cuatro entidades elegibles que reciben fondos del programa CSBG en Puerto Rico experimentó retrasos significativos en el desembolso inicial correspondiente al año fiscal 2025-2026. En su carta, el comisionado residente solicitó un desglose de las fechas en que ODSEC recibió las asignaciones federales, formalizó los acuerdos de subvención y desembolsó los fondos correspondientes a los años fiscales 2025, 2026 y, si está disponible, 2027. También requirió una explicación de cualquier retraso significativo y de las razones que lo provocaron. El Comisionado Residente solicitó que ODSEC entregue una respuesta escrita completa no más tarde del 26 de septiembre de 2026.

“ODSEC recibe fondos federales para combatir la pobreza y los desembolsa a varias entidades. Hemos recibido quejas de que se están atrasando. Esto afecta a la gente necesitada de Puerto Rico y queremos saber por qué se tardan y ayudar a resolver el problema”, dijo el comisionado residente”.

###
title: Comisionado Residente: ODSEC aguanta millones en fondos federales para combatir la pobreza

Tonight, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) will be hosting her fourth Congressional Commendation Ceremony, recognizing a group of outstanding El Pasoans whose work has strengthened the community across fields including education, public service, the arts, science, and advocacy.

“It is a privilege as our community’s federal representative to recognize the strength, resilience, and talent of our honorees,” said Congresswoman Escobar. "El Paso is grateful for their contributions and we are proud to celebrate the profound impact each of these individuals has made on our beloved community."

Information on each of the honorees (listed in alphabetical order) can be found below:

Beatriz Landin created the Wander Pillow, a neck pillow with a blanket stored inside that was featured on Amazon Prime Video’s “The Blox”.

Blueberry Carrillo gained national recognition by winning the prestigious Dav Pilkey Silver Medal Portfolio Award in June. She was one in twelve in the nation selected and the only student from Texas to receive the award in the Art category.

El Dorado High School’s “The Legend” yearbook staff was named a Columbia Scholastic Press Association Gold Crown Award recipient in 2024 for its 2023 yearbook “Como Cuando”.

Jose Hurtado, Ph.D is a UTEP professor in the Department of Earth, Environmental and Resource Sciences and a member of NASA’s Artemis II and II Science Teams. He earned a prestigious grant through the Lunar Mapping Program, supported by NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey to create high-quality, modern geologic maps of the moon.

Karime Lopez is student leader and innovator in STEM education. In May, she won the FIRST Leadership Award at the 2026 FIRST Robotics World Championship.

Manuela Alejandra Gomez, Ph.D. was appointed as one of only 12 internationally recognized scholars to serve as an advisor and research associate for the Moses Mesoamerican Archive and Research Project at Harvard University.

Marco Sanchez is a student at Harmony School of Innovation is a STEM driven civic leader from El Paso, Texas and is the Founder and President of Harmony Robotics Organization. He founded the El Paso Youth Alliance, a student run organization with the mission to help young people participate in civic engagement and local government. He is an alumni of Congresswoman Escobar’s Congressional Youth Advisory Council.

Margie Salazar became CEO of FirstLight, the first woman CEO of a local major credit union. In March, she was named the 2026 Remarkable Woman for El Paso, a program is designed to spotlight women who lead, inspire and forge a path for others in their communities.

Noel Candelaria is a special education teacher in Ysleta Independent School District. He currently serves as Vice President of the National Education Association, the nation's largest labor union representing more than three million educators.

Retired Command Sergeant Major Janina Simmons made history in 2019 as the first Black woman to graduate from the U.S. Army Ranger School. Her accomplishments also include becoming an ultramarathon runner and a published author.

Shaheli De Silva is a student at Young Women’s STEAM Research and Preparatory Academy. Earlier this year, she won the Regional English Spelling Bee in English and tied for first in EPISD’s Spanish Spelling Bee.

WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Representatives Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09), Robin Kelly (IL-02), Nanette Barragán (CA-44), and Emily Randall (WA-06) led 49 Members of Congress in sending a letter to Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz calling for an immediate end to the sharing of Medicaid enrollee data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Despite a federal preliminary injunction limiting data transfers, CMS continues to share private data belonging to millions of enrollees—including U.S. citizens and lawful residents—beyond court-approved limits. Reports also reveal ICE improperly mishandled the data across internal channels and shared it with third-party analytics contractors like Palantir Technologies.

“The role of HHS should be to protect the health of all those living in this country and provide essential human services, not to be a watchdog for DHS or act as immigration enforcement,” the Members stated in the letter.

Read the full letter here.

Brownsville, Texas – Today, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) announced $2.5 million in federal funding for the City of Brownsville Public Works Department to support the design and construction of the Marina Industrial Park, including roadway, water, sewer and stormwater infrastructure. The funds are delivered through the U.S. Economic Development Administration (EDA) and estimated to create 590 new jobs and leverage over $18 million in private investment. The total projected cost of this project is $4,395,000.

“Brownsville has quickly become a prime attraction for American manufacturers and businesses to call our city home. We must have the transportation and infrastructure in place to meet these heightened demands for economic growth. This funding helps us get there while creating hundreds of new jobs and bringing millions of dollars in new opportunities to the Rio Grande Valley. When we invest in local development, we invest in the future of South Texas,” said Congressman Gonzalez.

“Brownsville is attracting new industries, creating quality jobs, and strengthening its role as a leading hub for international trade and manufacturing. This $2.5 million federal investment in the Marina Industrial Park will further support our effort to build the critical infrastructure needed to support that growth, while leveraging more than $18 million in private investment and creating new jobs. We are grateful to Congressman Gonzalez and the U.S. Economic Development Administration for recognizing Brownsville’s economic potential and investing in our community’s future,” said Mayor John Cowen, Jr., City of Brownsville.

The Marina Industrial Park will include five state-of-the-art multi-tenant industrial buildings: four buildings of 150,000 square feet each and one slightly smaller facility of 140,000 square feet. Located on FM 511 in Brownsville’s northern industrial corridor, the new Industrial Park is an ideal gateway for manufacturers to supply goods across North America as it is near two interstate highways, four international bridges, the Port of Brownsville, three international airports, and a U.S.-Mexico rail crossing.

NASHVILLE, TN — Today, Tuesday, September 8, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) and Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY-21) announced the launch of the new bipartisan Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus while visiting Vanderbilt University. The caucus aims to hold colleges and universities accountable for protecting Jewish students, faculty, and staff.

The Representatives announced the formation of the caucus during a conversation at Vanderbilt University featuring Vanderbilt Chancellor Daniel Diermeier and five visiting university leaders from across the country, including leaders from The University of Kentucky, The University of Texas at Austin, Dartmouth College, The University of Alabama, and Washington University in St. Louis. The panel discussed how their campuses are working to combat antisemitism while protecting free expression.

“Since October 7th, Jewish students on too many campuses have been harassed, intimidated, and made to feel like strangers in their own school,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That’s why Elise and I are teaming up to launch this caucus to hold universities accountable, back up the schools getting it right, like Vanderbilt, and make sure every Jewish kid can have a college experience without fear of discrimination or violence.”

“From asking questions at the most watched hearing in Congressional history with university presidents that led to an earthquake in higher education to passing key legislation, I have been proud to be the leader in Congress on combatting antisemitism and anti-Americanism at our colleges and universities,” said Congresswoman Elise Stefanik (NY- 21). “I am proud to launch this bipartisan Congressional Caucus with my friend and colleague Representative Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) who has been a leading partner and legislator with whom I have worked on this critical issue. We are committed to saving American higher education for the next generation.”

Since the October 7, 2023 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel, antisemitism on American college campuses has surged to levels never before recorded. According to the Anti-Defamation League, antisemitic incidents on campuses spiked more than 300 percent in 2023 alone, followed by a further sharp rise in 2024, with well over a thousand incidents logged in the year after October 7th. The vast majority of Jewish college students say they have personally witnessed or experienced antisemitism since that day.

The Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus will:

Serve as a bipartisan forum for Members of Congress to coordinate oversight of how colleges and universities respond to antisemitism.

Press institutions to protect Jewish students, faculty, and staff, and to enforce their own anti-harassment and anti-discrimination policies.

Advance and track federal legislation targeting campus antisemitism and BDS-driven discrimination, including the Antisemitism Awareness Act, the HEAL Act, and the newly House-passed Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act.

Spotlight schools that are getting it right and share best practices across campuses nationwide.

Gottheimer has been a leading voice in Congress against antisemitism, including:

Authoring the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which directs the Department of Education to use the IHRA working definition of antisemitism when enforcing federal anti-discrimination law. The bill passed the House 320–91 last Congress.

Helping pass the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act, restricting federal student aid to colleges that engage in commercial BDS boycotts of Israel. The bill cleared the House 237–169 on September 3rd and now heads to the Senate.

Authoring the HEAL Act (Holocaust Education and Antisemitism Lessons Act) and the October 7th Remembrance Education Act to strengthen Holocaust and October 7th education in schools.

Leading H.Res. 883, declaring the “from the river to the sea” chant antisemitic, and the IGO Anti-Boycott Act, both of which have passed the House.

Pressing university presidents directly, sending letters to schools including Rutgers, Columbia, Harvard, Penn, MIT, Princeton, Brown, GW, and NYU demanding concrete plans to protect Jewish students.

Serving as a member of the House Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism.

Below: Gottheimer announces Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus at Vanderbilt University.

Press Contact
